beats.role_note: COLD OPEN LAW — open on the Claude composer, ask shown ANSWERED
beats.narration_text: Cardiac admissions, a mortality model built from the chart, and one routine test sitting in the record. The question is whether adding it helps.

props.command:
claude "MIMIC-IV cardiac admissions + MIMIC-IV-ECG.
  Does adding the ECG improve in-hospital mortality prediction?
  Patient-grouped CV, cluster bootstrap over patients."
props.segment: A Stale ECG Is Worse Than No ECG

beats.role_note: the stakes, stated BEFORE the build begins. No composer chrome.
beats.narration_text: On its own that answer looks boring. Two thousandths of a point. Nobody ships a change that small. But it is an average over a hundred and forty-four thousand admissions, and it is hiding a sign flip. Some of those ECGs were taken the same day the patient arrived. Some were three years old. The model cannot tell the difference, because nothing in the feature vector says how old the evidence is.
beats.visual_intent: The aggregate trap: one flat +0.0021 bar holds the frame, then splits into four bins of wildly different sign. The average is shown to be a mixture, not a measurement.
beats.new_visual_element: EcgAverageTrap — average splits into four signed bins

beats.role_note: composer — SPARK-LINE LAW: greeting is 'The ask,'
beats.narration_text: So the first ask is a split, not a summary. Bin every admission by how old its ECG was at the moment of admission, and put an interval on each bin. One detail matters more than it looks. Resample patients, not admissions. Patients come back, and an admission-level split leaks the same person across the fold boundary.

props.command:
claude "bin admissions by ECG age at admittime.
  per-bin delta AUROC (EHR+ECG minus EHR).
  StratifiedGroupKFold on subject_id — patients recur.
  cluster bootstrap over PATIENTS, 1000 replicates.
  test the decay, don't eyeball four intervals."
props.segment: A Stale ECG Is Worse Than No ECG

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — real source from src/analyze.py, trimmed to the lines that teach
beats.narration_text: This is the resampling loop. It draws patients with replacement, rebuilds the table from that draw, and recomputes every bin inside the same replicate. Doing it in one loop is the point. It keeps the bins correlated, so the difference between two of them is a quantity you can put an interval on. The slope against log gap comes off the same draw. Four separate error bars side by side are not a test. This is.

props.title: src/analyze.py — cluster_bootstrap()
props.code:
# bin centres on a log scale, for the slope
x = np.array([np.log10(np.median(gap[b == k]) + 1)
              for k in range(len(BIN_LABELS))])

for i in range(n):                      # n = 1000 replicates
    pick = rng.integers(0, len(uniq), size=len(uniq))
    idx  = np.concatenate([rows_by_pat[j] for j in pick])

    d = _delta_by_bin(y, p_base, p_full, b, idx)
    draws[i]    = d
    contrast[i] = d[FRESH_BIN] - d[STALE_BIN]   # <- the test
    slope[i]    = np.polyfit(x[ok], d[ok], 1)[0]

beats.role_note: MOVING output beat. REBUILD LAW: fig2 rebuilt native, never screenshotted. Humanitarians palette per ASK->RESULT LAW.
beats.narration_text: Here is the split. A same-day ECG adds four and a half thousandths, and the interval clears zero. An ECG over a year old subtracts five thousandths, and that interval clears zero too, in the other direction. Worse than leaving the ECG out entirely. The two middle bins are drawn hatched on purpose. They are underpowered, not null. Their minimum detectable effect is larger than the effect they would need to find, so the honest reading is that we cannot tell, and the chart is required to say so rather than let you read a trend into it.
beats.visual_intent: Four bars grow from a zero baseline: fresh teal above the line, >1yr burnt-orange below it. Middle two render hatched grey with an 'underpowered' label. CI whiskers draw last. The zero line is the hero.
beats.new_visual_element: EcgStalenessBars — delta AUROC by ECG age, CIs, hatched underpowered bins

beats.role_note: THE REVISION LAW — check the output, name the flaw, type the revised ask. greeting 'The revision,'
beats.narration_text: Except that comparison is between different people. A patient with a same-day ECG is being actively worked up. A patient whose newest ECG is two years old came in for something nobody ordered an ECG for. Case mix alone could produce the whole pattern. So the revision is to stop comparing patients to each other, and compare a patient to themselves.

props.command:
claude "the bins are confounded by case mix.
  keep admissions with BOTH a same-day ECG and older ones.
  score the SAME rows repeatedly, feeding progressively
  older ECGs from that same patient.
  hold rows, labels and EHR features fixed."
props.segment: A Stale ECG Is Worse Than No ECG

beats.role_note: ACTUAL-CODE LAW — real source from src/within_patient.py
beats.narration_text: Train once on the fresh ECG, then score the same rows again and again, feeding the model progressively older ECGs belonging to that same patient. Same rows, same labels, same chart features. Notice the fitted model is reused rather than refitted. That is what makes this an ablation instead of another comparison. The only thing that changes between conditions is the age of one input.

props.title: src/within_patient.py — oof_cross_lag()
props.code:
for tr, te in cv.split(Xtrain_src, y, groups):
    # ONE model, trained once on the chosen lag, then shown
    # each ECG age in turn. Reusing the fitted object is what
    # makes this a clean ablation: the only thing differing
    # across conditions is the input.
    m = fit_model(Xtrain_src.iloc[tr][m_cols], y[tr])

    for L in lag_vals:                  # 0, 30, 180, 365 days
        oof[L][te] = m.predict_proba(
            X_by_lag[L].iloc[te][m_cols])[:, 1]

    # EHR-only reference on the SAME rows
    oof_ehr[te] = fit_predict(ehr.iloc[tr], y[tr], ehr.iloc[te])

beats.role_note: MOVING output beat. REBUILD LAW: fig6 rebuilt native. The payoff.
beats.narration_text: Forty thousand admissions, sixteen thousand patients, and the effect survives. Same patient, same admission, same outcome. Show the model an ECG from that morning and it gains five and a half thousandths. Show it one from about five hundred days earlier and it loses five thousandths, with the interval excluding zero. The line crosses into negative territory somewhere around two weeks. This is not case mix. It is the age of the evidence.
beats.visual_intent: Log-time x-axis, 2 hours to 3 years. Point at lag 0 sits in the teal 'helps' band; the line walks down and crosses the zero rule into the orange 'worse than nothing' band. CI whiskers on each point. The zero crossing is the moment.
beats.new_visual_element: EcgWithinPatientDecay — value vs no-ECG across ECG age, crossing zero

props.sparkLine: Same patient. Only the age changed.

beats.role_note: split from the original 42s B08 per duration-planner (two ideas, over the split ceiling). This half: WHY it happens.
beats.narration_text: The mechanism is a train-deploy mismatch. The model learned to trust the ECG because in training most ECGs were fresh, then it applied that trust to an input whose reliability had quietly changed underneath it. Train the same model on stale ECGs instead and it stops trusting them, landing back at chart-only performance. So the harm is not in old ECGs. It is in unearned trust.
beats.visual_intent: Train-deploy mismatch as two stacked age distributions: training mass piled at fresh, deployment mass spread out to years. The model's trust curve is fitted to the first and applied to the second. The reverse-training check sits beneath as the falsifier.

beats.role_note: split half two: what did NOT work. DOUBLE-CHECK LAW — reported as a negative result, never as a solution.
beats.narration_text: The obvious fix is to tell the model how old the ECG is. We tried that. It did not clearly work. Every interval crossed zero. Matching the training age mix to deployment looked better on the point estimate, but its interval crossed zero as well. Both are reported as negative results, not as fixes. Demonstrating the problem turned out to be the easy part.
beats.visual_intent: Two attempted remedies as labelled intervals on a zero rule; both straddle it. A stamp reads INCONCLUSIVE, not SOLVED. The zero line is the verdict.

beats.role_note: HANDOFF LAW — the prompt is READ ALOUD and discussed, never merely typed. greeting 'Your turn.'
beats.narration_text: Your turn. Take a model you actually run and pick its most important input. Then ask a question you probably have not asked it: how old is that value at the moment you score, compared to how old it was in training. If those two distributions differ, you have the same setup. Bin your validation set by the age of that feature and check whether the effect changes sign. Here is a prompt to start with.

props.command:
claude "for my deployed model: pick the most important feature.
  compute its AGE at scoring time vs in the training set.
  bin the validation set by that age.
  report delta-metric per bin with a cluster bootstrap,
  and flag any bin whose MDE exceeds the fresh-bin effect."
